'''Stuart J. Firestein''' is the chair of the Department of Biological Sciences at [[Columbia College, Columbia University|Columbia University]], where his laboratory is researching the [[vertebrate]] [[olfactory receptor neuron]]. He has published articles in ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' magazine,<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Firestein |first=Stuart |title=Doubt Is Good for Science, But Bad for PR |url=https://www.wired.com/2012/07/firestein-science-doubt/ |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired Magazine]] |access-date=2012-11-28}}</ref> ''[[Huffington Post]]'',<ref>{{cite web |title=Stuart Firestein |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/stuart-firestein |publisher=[[HuffPost]] |accessdate=2012-11-28}}</ref> and ''[[Scientific American]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Firestein |first=Stuart |title=What Science Wants to Know An impenetrable mountain of facts can obscure the deeper questions |url=http://bioweb.biology.columbia.edu/firestein/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/What-Science-Wants-to-Know-Scientific-American-April-2012.pdf |publisher=[[Scientific American]] Magazine |accessdate=2012-11-28}}</ref> Firestein has been elected as a fellow by the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) for his meritorious efforts to advance science. He is an adviser to the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] program for the Public Understanding of Science.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tribeca Film Institute and the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation Announce 2011 TFI Sloan Filmmaker Fund Recipients |url=http://www.tribecafilminstitute.org/about/press/119625154.html |publisher=[[Tribeca Film Institute]] |accessdate=2012-11-28}}</ref>  Firestein's writing often advocates for better science writing.<ref>{{cite web |last=Firestein |first=Stuart |title=We Need a Crash Course in Citizen Science |date=11 May 2012 |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/stuart-firestein/science-public-funding_b_1510214.html |publisher=HuffPost |accessdate=2012-12-29}}</ref>  In 2012 he released the book ''Ignorance: How it Drives Science'', and in 2015, ''Failure: Why Science Is So Successful''.

==Early life==
Firestein was raised in [[Philadelphia]]. As a child, Firestein had many interests. In an interview with a reporter for Columbia College, he described his early history. "I started out with the usual childhood things — cowboy, fireman. My first interests were in science. I wanted to be an astronomer." Firestein attended an all-boys middle school, a possible reason he became interested in theater arts, because they were able to interact with an all-girls school. Firestein worked in theater for almost 20 years in San Francisco and Los Angeles and [[Repertory Theatre|rep]] companies on the East Coast. At the age of 30, Firestein enrolled in [[San Francisco State]] as a full-time student.  He has credited an animal communication class with Professor Hal Markowitz as "the most important thing that happened to me in life." Firestein received his graduate degree at age 40.<ref name="FiveMinutes">{{cite web |last=Rouen |first=Ethan |title=Five Minutes with … Stuart Firestein |url=http://www.college.columbia.edu/cct/mar_apr10/around_the_quads2 |publisher=[[Columbia College, Columbia University|Columbia College]] |accessdate=2012-11-28}}</ref>

==Career==
After earning his Ph.D. in [[neurobiology]], Firestein was a researcher at [[Yale Medical School]], then joined [[Columbia University]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.columbia.edu/research/2779 |title=Prof. Stuart Firestein Explains Why Ignorance Is Central to Scientific Discovery |publisher=[[Columbia University]] |date=May 9, 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150624182933/http://news.columbia.edu/research/2779 |archive-date=June 24, 2015 }}</ref>

At the Columbia University Department of Biological Sciences, Firestein is now studying the sense of smell. In his neuroscience lab, they investigate how the brain works, using the nose as a "model system" to understand the smaller piece of a difficult complex brain.

===''Ignorance: How It Drives Science''===
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right |
headerimage=[[File:Stuart Firestein 7-13-2012.JPG|210px]] | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nq0_zGzSc8g Stuart Firestein: The pursuit of ignorance], (18:33), [[TED (conference)|TED talks]]
| video2 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kq2iuc7juB8 Ignorance: The Birthsplace of Bang: Stuart Firestein at TEDxBrussels], (16:29)
}}
In his 2012 book ''Ignorance: How It Drives Science'', Firestein argues that pursuing research based on what we don't know is more valuable than building on what we do know. When asked why he wrote the book, Firestein replied, "I came to the realization at some point several years ago that these kids [his students] must actually think we know all there is to know about neuroscience. And that's the difference. That's not what we think in the lab. What we think in the lab is, we don't know bupkis. So I thought, well, we should be talking about what we don't know, not what we know."<ref name="DailyBeast">{{cite news |last=Schwartz |first=Casey |title=Stuart Firestein, Author of 'Ignorance,' Says Not Knowing Is the Key to Science |url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2012/04/22/stuart-firestein-author-of-ignorance-says-not-knowing-is-the-key-to-science.html |website=[[The Daily Beast]] |date=22 April 2012 |accessdate=2012-11-28}}</ref>  The book was largely based on his class on ignorance, where each week he invited a professor from the hard sciences to lecture for two hours on what they do not know.  No audio-visuals and no prepared lectures were allowed, the lectures became free-flowing conversations that students participated in.

Firestein explained to talk show host [[Diane Rehm]] that most people believe ignorance precedes knowledge, but in science, ignorance follows knowledge. Knowledge enables scientists to propose and pursue interesting questions about data that sometimes don't exist or fully make sense yet. "I use that term purposely to be a little provocative. But I don't mean stupidity. I don't mean dumb. I don't mean a callow indifference to facts or data or any of that," Firestein said. Instead, thoughtful ignorance looks at gaps in a community's understanding and seeks to resolve them.<ref name="DianeRehm">{{cite web |last=Rehm |first=Diane |title=Stuart Firestein: "Ignorance How it Drives Science" |url=http://thedianerehmshow.org/shows/2012-05-22/stuart-firestein-ignorance-how-it-drives-science |publisher=The [[Diane Rehm]] Show |accessdate=2012-11-28}}</ref>

===Scientific method===
The scientific method is a huge mistake, according to Firestein. He says that a hypothesis should be made after collecting data, not before. Firestein claims that scientists fall in love with their own ideas to the point that their own biases start dictating the way they look at the data. Oddly, he feels that facts are sometimes the most unreliable part of research. He feels that scientists don't know all the facts perfectly, and they "don't know them forever."<ref name="DianeRehm" />

===Searching for a black cat in a dark room===
According to Firestein, scientific research is like trying to find a black cat in a dark room: It's very hard to find it, "especially when there's no black cat." His thesis is that the field of science has many black rooms where scientists freely move from one to another once the lights are turned on. Another analogy he uses is that scientific research is like a puzzle without a guaranteed solution.<ref name="DianeRehm" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Blakeslee |first=Sandra |title=To Advance, Search for a Black Cat in a Dark Room |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/06/19/science/ignorance-book-review-scientists-dont-care-for-facts.html?_r=0 |newspaper=[[New York Times]] |date=18 June 2012 |accessdate=2013-01-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=BookTV: Stuart Firestein, "Ignorance: How it Drives Science" | date=9 July 2012 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z27OrDsCk8c |publisher=[[Book TV]] |accessdate=2013-01-06}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Firestein is married to [[Diana Reiss]], a cognitive psychologist at [[Hunter College]] and the [[City University of New York]], where she studies animal behavior.

* 2011 Lenfest Distinguished Columbia Faculty Award for excellence in scholarship and teaching<ref>{{cite web |url=http://worldsciencefestival.com/participants/stuart_firestein |title=Stuart Firestein |accessdate=September 3, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Eight profs receive Columbia's top teaching award |url=http://magazine.columbia.edu/news/spring-2011/eight-profs-receive-columbia%E2%80%99s-top-teaching-award |publisher=Columbia Magazine |accessdate=2012-11-28}}</ref>
